newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan approves fifth China shipper for direct link.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan approves fifth China shipper for direct link.

text.p: Taiwan on Wednesday approved a fifth shipping firm from China for direct voyages to the Nationalist-ruled island, but Beijing said its approval for Taipei shippers may not be announced before the end of April.
Port authorities in the southern Taiwanese city of Kaohsiung gave the nod for China's Fuzhou Mawei Shipping Co to make the direct crossing of the Taiwan Strait after a 48-year-old ban.
"Mawei had all its documents ready, so we approved it without any difficulties," Kaohsiung port official Deng You-yi told Reuters.
Despite Taiwan's approval, the likely end of the ban on direct Taiwan-China shipping links remained uncertain as Beijing has yet to approve any Taiwan shipping firms' applications.

"The date for the first ship to cross the Taiwan strait has not yet been decided, but it is likely to be known by the end of this month," an official of the Taiwan Affairs Office of the Ministry of Communications said in Beijing on Wednesday.
He said ministry officials were considering applications from about a dozen Taiwan shipping companies for approval to ply direct routes, but declined to give further details.
Analysts said Taiwan's Yangming Marine Transport Corp, Uniglory Marine, Wan Hai Lines and Chinese Maritime Transport Ltd were likely to be selected for direct links to the mainland.

Taipei's China Times on Wednesday quoted mainland sources as saying the Sheng Da, owned by China's Fujian Provincial Shipping Co but registered in Saint Vincent, would depart Xiamen for Kaohsiung on Thursday.
An official of the Fujian Xiamen Shipping Co based in the southern port of Xiamen which is opposite Taiwan, denied knowledge of this.
"We have no information about when we will be able to sail across the Taiwan strait," the official said.

"The report that a Chinese ship will sail to Taiwan on Thursday is a rumour," he said by telephone, adding that the company had purchased the vessel Sheng Da recently, expressly to engage in cross-strait shipping.

The Sheng Da is one of four ships from four other mainland sea freight firms approved by Taiwan on April 11 to sail directly into Kaohsiung from the mainland in an easing of a ban on direct links dating to the civil war that split them in 1949.

Nationalist-ruled Taiwan denies that the long-forbidden crossings are direct links because mainland cargoes will not be allowed to enter Taiwan customs. Rather, they can only be processed at what Taiwan is calling an "offshore transshipment centre" for onward passage to third countries.
Taiwan cargoes at Kaohsiung cannot be put aboard ships planning to cross directly to two mainland ports approved for the scheme -- Xiamen and the Fujian capital of Fuzhou.
The four approved mainland shippers are Fujian Foreign Trade Centre Shipping Co, Fujian Provincial Shipping Co, Fujian Xiamen Shipping Co and Shamen Ocean Shipping Co.
Taiwan proposed the offshore transshipment scheme in 1995 in a strategy to ensure direct crossings do not undermine the sovereignty of its exiled Republic of China.
Beijing, taking a different tack, says the routes are domestic links between two provinces, one of which, Taiwan, remains under control of a renegade government.
